title: Mapping cellular targets of covalent cancer drugs in the entire mammalian body
abstract: As our understanding of biological systems reaches single-cell and high spatial resolutions, it becomes imperative that pharmacological approaches match this precision to understand drug actions. This need is particularly urgent for the targeted covalent inhibitors that are currently re-entering the stage for cancer treatments. By leveraging the unique kinetics of click reactions, we developed volumetric clearing-assisted tissue click chemistry (vCATCH) to enable deep and homogeneous click labeling across the three-dimensional (3D) mammalian body. With simple and passive incubation steps, vCATCH offers cellular-resolution drug imaging in the entire adult mouse. We combined vCATCH with hydrogel-based reinforcement of three-dimensional imaging solvent-cleared organs (HYBRiD) imaging and virtual reality to visualize and quantify in vivo targets of two clinical cancer drugs, afatinib and ibrutinib, which recapitulated their known pharmacological distribution and revealed previously unreported tissue and cell-type engagement potentially linked to off-target effects. vCATCH provides a body-wide, unbiased platform to map covalent drug engagements at unprecedented scale and precision.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This Cell article is already showing early methodological uptake: it has 8 OpenAlex citations, 9 documented reuse events, and a notable downstream footprint in review and methods-oriented venues. The work’s core contribution is a body-wide in vivo mapping approach for covalent cancer drugs, and the citation landscape suggests it is being read as a platform method rather than a single-application study.

Full narrative

The paper’s strongest signal is its role as a methodological anchor. The record shows 16 RRIDs associated with the article, a marker that the work is being tied to reusable research resources and protocols. That fits the paper’s central advance: vCATCH, a click-chemistry-based strategy designed to enable deep, homogeneous tissue labeling for mapping cellular targets across the mammalian body. The article is framed around a clear translational need in covalent cancer therapeutics, where understanding drug distribution and target engagement in vivo is often technically limited.

Its downstream citation profile supports that framing. The 8 citations collected so far are concentrated in 2026 and span journals such as Nature Biotechnology, Journal of the American Chemical Society, ChemBioChem, Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, Nature Reviews Cancer, Trends in Pharmacological Sciences, Journal of Controlled Release, and Immunopharmacology and Immunotoxicology. That mix points to interest across chemical biology, drug discovery, oncology, and delivery-focused communities, with review coverage appearing alongside primary research uptake.

The reuse record is also meaningful. Beyond scholarly citations, the article is documented as reused 9 times, including one Europe PMC biomedical article mention. The citing topics cluster around click chemistry, protein degradation and inhibitors, fluorescence microscopy, and biotin-related studies, reinforcing that the paper is being taken up as a technical resource with relevance beyond its immediate cancer-drug application. A separate Nature Reviews Cancer piece explicitly discusses vCATCH as enabling body-wide in vivo drug distribution mapping, which further indicates that the method is already entering broader expert synthesis.

The surrounding stewardship signals are consistent with a platform paper that was designed for reuse. The work is associated with a GitHub repository, and Crossref’s data-citation checks indicate the article is being cited as a dataset as well as a paper. Funding support from NIH institutes, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, and other sources suggests substantial infrastructure behind the method, while the hybrid open-access status should help with accessibility. At this stage, the record is still early, so the main story is not volume but positioning: the paper is being recognized as a reusable in vivo mapping method for covalent drug biology, with citation and reuse patterns that align with that role.
